chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

notes.overview: This chapter traces how the idea of nationalism emerged in 19th-century Europe and led to the unification of Italy and Germany, and eventually to the redrawing of Europe's political map after the First World War. Nationalism is the belief that people who share a common language, culture, history or ethnicity should form a single, self-governing nation-state.
key_points: France under Napoleon spread many nationalist ideas (Civil Code, uniform laws, abolition of feudal privileges) even while acting as a conqueror.
The Congress of Vienna (1815), led by Metternich of Austria, tried to restore conservative monarchies after Napoleon's defeat and suppress nationalist movements.
Liberal nationalism in the early 19th century stood for individual freedom, equality before law, and constitutional government, alongside national self-determination.
The Romantic movement (Herder, Fichte) emphasised a shared collective heritage, folklore, language and culture as the true spirit (Volksgeist) of a nation.
Economic factors mattered: the Zollverein (customs union) of 1834 removed tariff barriers between German states and created a sense of shared economic interest, paving the way for unification.
Italy was unified between 1859-1870 through the efforts of Mazzini (ideologue), Cavour (diplomat, Sardinia-Piedmont's Prime Minister) and Garibaldi (military leader of the Red Shirts).

Germany was unified in 1871 under Otto von Bismarck, Chancellor of Prussia, through three wars (against Denmark, Austria, and France) - a process called 'unification from above' led by the army and bureaucracy rather than a popular movement.
Nationalism also had a darker, exclusionary side: it fuelled visions of national superiority and was used to justify aggression, culminating in extreme forms in the 20th century.
After the First World War, the map of Europe was redrawn based on the principle of national self-determination, breaking up the multi-national Habsburg, Ottoman and Russian empires.

key_terms.Nationalism: A sense of political and cultural unity based on a shared identity, aspiring to a sovereign nation-state.
key_terms.Plebiscite: A direct vote by the people on a single political question, used to decide territorial annexation.
key_terms.Zollverein: A customs union formed in 1834 joining most German states to remove tariff barriers.
key_terms.Utopian: A vision of a society so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist; used for early socialist thinkers.
key_terms.Suffrage: The right to vote in political elections.

important_facts: Unification of Germany: 1871 (Proclaimed at the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles)

sections.title: 1. Frederic Sorrieu's Vision (1848)
sections.content: In 1848, the French artist Frederic Sorrieu prepared a series of prints imagining a world of democratic and social republics, peopled by people of all ages and social classes, marching in procession to pay homage to the Statue of Liberty. Broken and scattered objects lying on the ground symbolise the defeated absolutist monarchies. Each nation is represented by its own flag and national costume, showing Sorrieu's utopian vision of a world made up of independent nation-states founded on the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity.

sections.title: 2. The French Revolution and the Birth of Nationalism (1789)
sections.content: The French Revolution of 1789 marked the first clear expression of nationalism, ending absolute monarchy and declaring that sovereignty resided in the people, not the king. Citizens became active participants in shaping the nation's destiny. Measures such as a centralised administrative system, uniform laws, abolition of internal customs duties (octroi), and the adoption of a common language (French) and the tricolour flag helped create a sense of collective identity among the French people. The ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity inspired nationalists across Europe throughout the nineteenth century.

sections.title: 3. Napoleon Bonaparte and the Napoleonic Code (1804)
sections.content: After the revolutionary years, Napoleon Bonaparte came to power in France and, through his conquests, carried revolutionary administrative ideas across Europe. His Civil Code of 1804, popularly called the Napoleonic Code, abolished privileges based on birth, established equality before the law, and secured the right to property. He simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, and standardised weights, measures and currency. However, increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription into the French army bred resentment, and his rule paradoxically strengthened nationalist sentiment among the very peoples he conquered.

sections.title: 4. Europe After 1815: The Congress of Vienna and Conservative Restoration
sections.content: After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, European powers met at the Congress of Vienna under the guidance of the Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich to undo most of the changes brought by the revolution and restore conservative monarchies. Conservatives believed in preserving traditional institutions - the monarchy, the church, social hierarchies, property and the family - but did accept some modernisation to strengthen autocracy. The Treaty of Vienna redrew the map of Europe (e.g. the German confederation of 39 states, restoration of the Bourbon dynasty in France) to check future French expansion, but the forces of nationalism this order tried to suppress continued to grow underground.

sections.title: 5. Liberalism and the Middle Class
sections.content: The word 'liberalism' comes from the Latin 'liber', meaning free. For the new middle classes - industrialists, businessmen and professionals - liberalism stood politically for the end of autocracy, equality before the law, and government by consent through an elected parliament, functioning under a constitution. Economically, liberalism championed free markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital. However, liberal political rights were not universal - voting rights were largely limited to property-owning men, and women and the poor were mostly excluded, which became a source of continuing struggle through the nineteenth century.

sections.title: 6. Romanticism, Culture and the Idea of the Volk
sections.content: Alongside liberal ideas, Romanticism - a cultural movement - sought to build a shared collective heritage as the basis of a nation. Romantic artists and poets criticised the excessive emphasis on reason and science, focusing instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings. German philosophers Johann Gottfried Herder and Johann Gottlieb Fichte argued that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people - das Volk - through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances. Collecting and recording local folklore was thus seen as essential to recovering the true spirit of the nation, as done famously by the Grimm brothers.

sections.title: 7. Economic Nationalism: The Zollverein (1834)
sections.content: Nationalism was not only about culture and politics but also economics. In 1834, a customs union or Zollverein was formed at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, creating a network of railways that further stimulated mobility, and fostering a sense of economic oneness among German-speaking states even before political unification. This economic integration built the foundation on which the eventual political unification of Germany under Prussian leadership would be constructed.

sections.title: 8. The Revolutions of 1830 and 1848
sections.content: Liberal-nationalist revolutions swept across Europe in 1830 and 1848. In 1830, the Bourbon kings of France were overthrown by liberal revolutionaries who installed a constitutional monarchy, and Greece won independence from Ottoman rule in 1832 after a long struggle supported by Romantic poets like Lord Byron. In 1848, a wave of revolutions led by the educated middle classes broke out across Europe, combining demands for constitutionalism with nationalist aspirations, most visibly in the Frankfurt Parliament, where German middle-class liberals drafted a constitution for a unified Germany headed by a monarchy subject to parliament - though this liberal initiative was eventually repressed by the combined forces of the monarchy and military.

sections.title: 9. The Unification of Italy (1859-1870)
sections.content: Before unification, Italy was divided into seven states, only one of which - Sardinia-Piedmont - was ruled by an Italian princely house. Giuseppe Mazzini founded the secret society Young Italy to spread the vision of a unified Italian republic. Count Camillo Cavour, the chief minister of Sardinia-Piedmont, engineered unification through diplomacy and an alliance with France to defeat Austria, without believing in democratic or republican ideals himself. Giuseppe Garibaldi led a volunteer army called the Red Shirts and, with popular support, conquered Southern Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. In 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of unified Italy.

sections.title: 10. The Unification of Germany (1866-1871)
sections.content: Nationalist feeling among the German middle classes was strong after the failed 1848 revolution, but political unification was ultimately achieved not through popular movements but through the leadership of Prussia's chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, aided by the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Bismarck fought three wars over seven years - against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870-71) - which ended in Prussian victory and completed unification. In January 1871, the Prussian king, Kaiser William I, was proclaimed German Emperor at a ceremony held in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, and the new state placed a strong emphasis on modernising currency, banking, legal and judicial systems.

sections.title: 11. Nationalism, Imperialism and the First World War
sections.content: By the last quarter of the nineteenth century, nationalism no longer retained its liberal-democratic sentiment of promoting freedom; instead, it became a narrow ideology used to justify imperialist expansion. The Balkans - a region of geographic and ethnic variety comprising modern-day Bosnia, Serbia, Albania, Romania, Macedonia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece - became an area of intense conflict as the Ottoman Empire declined and different Balkan nationalities struggled for independence, while the big European powers manoeuvred to expand their own territories in the region. This tangle of conflicting nationalist and imperialist ambitions in the Balkans was a major factor leading to the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.

In the Balkans especially, intense rivalries between European powers over territory and influence, fuelled by nationalist ambitions, created constant tension. This competitive, aggressive nationalism combined with imperial rivalry to become one of the major causes of the First World War.

questions.question: Describe the process of the unification of Germany under the leadership of Otto von Bismarck.

questions.model_answer: Nationalist feeling was strong among the German middle classes, who in 1848 had attempted to unite the many German-speaking states into a nation-state with a parliament, but this liberal initiative was repressed. Thereafter, Prussia, under its Chief Minister Otto von Bismarck, took over the leadership of the unification movement, aided by the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Bismarck fought three wars over seven years - with Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870-71) - which ended in Prussian victory and completed the process of unification. In January 1871, the Prussian king, Kaiser William I, was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony at Versailles. This process is often described as unification 'from above' because it was carried out through state power, war and diplomacy rather than through a broad-based democratic movement.

Consequently, collecting and recording local folklore was considered essential to recover a nation's true spirit and past, as done famously by the Grimm brothers with their collection of folk tales.

questions.topic: Unification of Italy and Germany compared
questions.question: Explain any four similarities or differences between the processes of unification of Italy and Germany.

rubric.point: Both Italy and Germany were unified in the second half of the 19th century (Italy by 1870, Germany by 1871)
Italy's unification involved a mix of popular movements (Mazzini, Garibaldi) and diplomacy (Cavour), while Germany's was led almost entirely 'from above' by Bismarck and the Prussian state

Germany's unification was achieved primarily through a series of wars fought by Prussia (against Denmark, Austria, France), while Italy's involved wars, uprisings and plebiscites across various regions
Both processes ended with the creation of a constitutional monarchy (Victor Emmanuel II in Italy, Kaiser William I in Germany) rather than a republic

questions.model_answer: Both Italy and Germany were unified in the second half of the 19th century - Italy by 1870 and Germany by 1871. However, Italy's unification combined popular nationalist movements, such as those inspired by Mazzini and led militarily by Garibaldi, with the diplomacy of Cavour, while Germany's unification was carried out almost entirely 'from above' under the leadership of Bismarck and the Prussian state and army. Germany's unification was achieved chiefly through a sequence of wars fought by Prussia against Denmark, Austria and France, whereas Italy's process involved a combination of wars, local uprisings and plebiscites across different Italian states. In both cases, the outcome was a constitutional monarchy rather than a republic - Victor Emmanuel II became king of a unified Italy, and Kaiser William I was proclaimed German Emperor.

questions.topic: Case study - the Frankfurt Parliament and the Revolutions of 1848
questions.passage: In 1848, a wave of political upheavals swept across Europe, led mostly by the educated middle classes. In the German regions, an all-German National Assembly convened in the Church of St Paul at Frankfurt, where 831 elected representatives drafted a constitution for a unified German nation to be headed by a constitutional monarchy. However, the Prussian king rejected the crown offered by this assembly, and the parliament - which had no support from the army or the masses - was eventually forced to disband.

questions.topic: 1848 as the Revolution of the Liberals in Europe
questions.question: Do you agree that the period of 1848 is considered a phase of the 'Revolution of the Liberals' in Europe? Elucidate with suitable examples.

rubric.point: In 1848, a revolution led by educated middle classes occurred alongside revolts of the poor, unemployed, peasants and workers across Europe; in France the monarch abdicated in February 1848 and a republic based on universal male suffrage was proclaimed

In Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, liberal middle-class men and women demanded a constitution and national unification, using popular unrest to push for a nation-state built on parliamentary principles

In the German-speaking areas, political associations convened the Frankfurt parliament (May 1848) in the Church of St Paul, drafted a constitution for a German nation under a constitutional monarch, but King Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown and the assembly (dominated by the middle class, having ignored artisans' and workers' demands) was eventually forced to disband by troops

Women actively participated in the liberal movement (forming political associations, newspapers) but were still denied suffrage and admitted to the Frankfurt assembly only as observers - showing the 'liberal' revolution's real limits

Concludes that 1848 can indeed be seen as a phase of the Revolution of the Liberals, since it was substantially driven by liberal middle-class demands for constitutions and nation-states, even though it ultimately failed to secure full liberal or democratic outcomes

questions.model_answer: Yes: in 1848, a revolution led by the educated middle classes swept across many European countries, alongside separate revolts by the poor, unemployed, peasants and workers. In France, the king abdicated in February 1848 and a republic based on universal male suffrage was declared. Elsewhere - in Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian empire - liberal middle-class men and women pushed for constitutions and national unification, using the wider popular unrest to advance demands for a nation-state built on parliamentary principles (a constitution, freedom of the press, freedom of association). In the German-speaking areas, political associations of middle-class professionals convened the Frankfurt parliament in May 1848 at the Church of St Paul and drafted a constitution for a German nation under a constitutional monarch, offering the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia - who rejected it and joined other monarchs against the assembly; having also ignored the demands of artisans and workers, the middle-class-dominated parliament lost popular support and was eventually disbanded by troops. Even the question of women's rights showed the movement's limits: despite active participation by women in political associations and journalism, women were denied suffrage and admitted to the Frankfurt assembly only as observers. Overall, 1848 fits the description of a 'Revolution of the Liberals' - substantially driven by liberal middle-class demands for constitutional, nation-based government - even though it ultimately fell short of full liberal or democratic success.

questions.topic: Growth of nationalist tensions in the Balkans before World War I
questions.question: Analyse the reasons for the growth of nationalist tensions in the Balkan region before the First World War.

rubric.point: The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation (modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro), broadly inhabited by Slavs, and much of it was under the control of the declining Ottoman Empire
The spread of romantic nationalism combined with the disintegration of Ottoman control made the region volatile, and one by one its subject nationalities broke away and declared independence
The Balkan states were fiercely jealous of one another, each hoping to gain territory at the expense of the others

The region also became the stage for big-power rivalry, with Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary each competing for trade, colonies and naval/military dominance, and each seeking to extend its own influence over the Balkans at the expense of rivals
This combination of internal nationalist rivalry and external great-power competition led to a series of Balkan wars and ultimately helped trigger the First World War

questions.model_answer: The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic diversity - covering modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro - whose inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs, and a large part of it lay under the control of the declining Ottoman Empire. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism, combined with the disintegration of Ottoman authority, made the region highly volatile, and one by one its subject nationalities broke away from Ottoman control and declared independence. The newly independent Balkan states were fiercely jealous of one another, each hoping to expand its territory at the others' expense. Matters were made worse because the Balkans also became a stage for rivalry among the European great powers - Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary - who were competing intensely over trade, colonies, and naval and military strength, and each sought to extend its own influence in the region while countering the others. This combustible mix of internal nationalist rivalries and external big-power competition led to a series of wars in the region, and ultimately helped trigger the First World War.

questions.question: Why did the Polish language become a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance in the later half of the nineteenth century? Explain.

rubric.point: Poland was partitioned among Russia, Prussia and Austria in the late 18th century, losing its independence
In Russian-controlled Poland, the Tsarist regime tried to impose the Russian language and suppress Polish language/culture as part of a Russification policy
Polish clergy and gentry defied these orders by continuing to use Polish in church and schools, even facing imprisonment or deportation, so the language became a symbol of nationalist resistance

questions.model_answer: Poland had been partitioned among Russia, Prussia and Austria in the late eighteenth century and lost its independence. In Russian-controlled Poland, the Tsarist government tried to suppress Polish culture and impose the Russian language as part of a policy of 'Russification'. Polish was removed from schools and administration, but the Polish clergy and gentry refused to use Russian in church and in teaching, defying these orders even at the risk of imprisonment or deportation to Siberia. Because of this defiance, the Polish language became a powerful symbol of the nationalist struggle against Russian domination.

questions.topic: Culture and the rise of nationalism
questions.question: Describe the role of culture in shaping the feelings of nationalism in Europe at the end of the nineteenth century.

rubric.point: Romanticism used art, poetry, stories, music and language to build shared national identity and a sense of a common past
Folk songs, folklore and dances were collected and revived as part of the national spirit (e.g. the Grimm brothers in Germany)
Language became central to nationalist feeling, as with the Polish resistance to Russification through language
Music, opera and visual symbols (personification of the nation, e.g. Marianne in France, Germania in Germany) evoked and popularised nationalist feeling

questions.model_answer: Culture played a central role in shaping nationalism through the Romantic movement, which emphasised emotion, intuition and mystical feeling over reason, and used art, poetry, stories and music to build a sense of shared national identity and a common past. Language and folklore were collected and revived to keep alive national feeling, as when the Grimm brothers gathered German folk tales, or when the Polish language became a symbol of resistance against Russification. Music and opera - such as those of Verdi in Italy - stirred patriotic emotion. Visual art too personified the nation, as with figures like Marianne in France and Germania in Germany, giving abstract nationalist ideas a concrete, emotionally powerful image that people could rally around.

questions.question: Describe the process of unification of Italy.

rubric.point: Italy was divided into seven states in the early 19th century, and only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian royal house; Mazzini's Young Italy pursued a unified republic but early revolts (1831, 1848) failed
Chief Minister Cavour led the movement under King Victor Emmanuel II - a diplomatic alliance with France defeated Austria in 1859, gaining Lombardy
Giuseppe Garibaldi led armed volunteers ('Redshirts') in 1860 to conquer southern Italy and Sicily, and through plebiscites these regions united with Sardinia-Piedmont
Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of united Italy in 1861; Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome in 1870, completing unification

questions.model_answer: In the early nineteenth century, Italy was divided into seven states, and only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian royal house. Giuseppe Mazzini's secret society Young Italy pursued the vision of a unified Italian republic, but revolts in 1831 and 1848 failed. Chief Minister Cavour then led the movement under King Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia-Piedmont, engineering a diplomatic alliance with France that defeated Austria in 1859 and won Lombardy. In 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi led his armed volunteers (the 'Redshirts') to conquer the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south, and through plebiscites these regions joined Sardinia-Piedmont. In 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of a united Italy. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome in 1870, completing the process of unification.

notes.overview: This chapter explains how the sense of belonging to one nation grew in India during the freedom struggle, largely through the leadership of the Indian National Congress under Mahatma Gandhi, and how diverse social groups participated in and interpreted the idea of Swaraj differently.
key_points: The First World War created a new economic and political situation in India - increased taxes, forced recruitment, and price rises caused widespread hardship, making people more receptive to Gandhi's call for mass mobilisation.
Gandhi returned to India in 1915 and first experimented with Satyagraha (non-violent civil resistance based on truth) in Champaran (Bihar, 1917), Kheda (Gujarat, 1918) and Ahmedabad (1918).
The Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed detention without trial; Gandhi launched a nationwide hartal against it, which led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar (13 April 1919).

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) urged Indians to surrender titles, boycott civil services, schools, courts and foreign goods; it merged with the Khilafat Movement led by the Ali brothers to unite Hindus and Muslims.
The movement was withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922) in Uttar Pradesh, where a violent mob set fire to a police station.
The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34) began with the Dandi March (Salt March), where Gandhi and followers walked about 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to break the salt law.

Different social groups joined the national movement with their own aspirations: rich peasants wanted lower revenue, poor peasants wanted rent relief, business classes wanted protection from foreign competition, and industrial workers had their own separate demands.
The idea of India as a nation was also constructed culturally through images (Bharat Mata by Abanindranath Tagore), folklore revival, and icons/symbols like the tricolour flag.
The Government of India Act 1935 and subsequent provincial elections (1937) deepened political participation but also sharpened communal politics, eventually contributing to the demand for Pakistan.

key_terms.Satyagraha: A method of non-violent resistance based on the power of truth and the search for justice.
key_terms.Swaraj: Self-rule or self-governance; Gandhi's term for genuine Indian independence.
key_terms.Boycott: Refusal to buy, use or participate in something (e.g., foreign goods, schools, courts) as a form of protest.
key_terms.Khilafat: A movement to protect the authority of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War, joined with the Non-Cooperation Movement.
key_terms.Civil Disobedience: Deliberate and public refusal to obey unjust laws, including breaking specific laws like the salt law.

important_facts: Dandi March / Civil Disobedience Movement begins: 12 March 1930
exam_tips: Learn the sequence: Rowlatt Act -> Jallianwala Bagh -> Non-Cooperation -> Chauri Chaura -> Civil Disobedience -> Salt March. Timeline questions are common.
Practice explaining why different social groups (peasants, workers, business class, women) participated in the movement - a favourite 5-mark question.
Be able to explain the significance of the salt march as a symbolic and effective form of protest.

sections.title: 1. The First World War and a New Political Situation
sections.content: The First World War (1914-18) created a new economic and political situation in India. Defence expenditure was financed through war loans and increased taxes; customs duties were raised and income tax introduced. Villages were forced to supply soldiers, and prices of goods doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing extreme hardship for the common people. A terrible influenza epidemic and successive crop failures added to the distress. This widespread suffering created the conditions in which Mahatma Gandhi's call for a united national struggle found mass appeal after his return to India in 1915.

sections.title: 2. Mahatma Gandhi and the Idea of Satyagraha
sections.content: Gandhi developed the technique of Satyagraha in South Africa, a novel method of mass agitation based on the power of truth and the search for justice without resorting to violence. Satyagraha held that if the cause was true and the struggle against injustice was conducted non-violently, oppressors would eventually be forced to recognise the truth, without being subjected to hatred that could turn into a battle. This idea emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for it, inviting even the opponent to accept that truth rather than be forced to accept it through violence.

sections.title: 3. Early Satyagraha Movements: Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad (1917-18)
sections.content: Gandhi's first major interventions in India tested Satyagraha at the local level. In 1917 he travelled to Champaran, Bihar, to inspire peasants to struggle against the oppressive indigo plantation system. In 1917 he organised a Satyagraha to support peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat, hit by crop failure and a plague epidemic, in their demand for revenue relief. In 1918, Gandhi went to Ahmedabad to organise a Satyagraha movement amongst cotton mill workers demanding better wages and working conditions. These early successes established Gandhi's leadership and his method as a viable tool of political mobilisation.

sections.title: 4. The Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919)
sections.content: In 1919, Gandhi launched a nationwide Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act (1919), which gave the colonial government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Rallies were organised in various cities, and a nationwide hartal (strike) was called on 6 April 1919. Alarmed at the popular response, local leaders were picked up and arrested in Amritsar, and Mahatma Gandhi was barred from entering Delhi. On 13 April 1919, a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar; General Dyer blocked the exits and ordered troops to open fire on the unarmed crowd, killing hundreds and shocking the nation, giving rise to widespread strikes, clashes with the police, and violent attacks on government buildings.

sections.title: 5. The Khilafat Movement and Hindu-Muslim Unity
sections.content: Indian Muslims were angered by rumours that a harsh peace treaty was going to be imposed on the Ottoman emperor, considered the spiritual head (Khalifa) of the Islamic world, after the First World War. A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919 under the leadership of the Ali brothers, Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, along with other leaders, to defend the Khalifa's authority. Gandhi saw this as a great opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement, and at the Calcutta session of the Congress in September 1920, leaders agreed to launch the Non-Cooperation Movement in support of Khilafat as well as for Swaraj.

sections.title: 6. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)
sections.content: Gandhi proposed that the Non-Cooperation Movement should unfold in stages, beginning with the surrender of government-conferred titles and honours, and a boycott of civil services, the army, police, courts, legislative councils, and government schools and colleges, followed eventually by non-payment of taxes if the government continued with repressive measures. The movement started with middle-class participation in the cities: students left schools, lawyers gave up their legal practices, and legislative council elections were boycotted, with the boycott of foreign cloth in favour of Indian khadi being especially powerful, though the movement's economic effects were partial as many continued attending schools and using courts.

sections.title: 7. Peasants, Tribals and Workers in the Movement
sections.content: Across the country, different social groups interpreted and joined the wider movement in their own ways. In Awadh, peasants led by Baba Ramchandra organised a struggle against talukdars and landlords demanding reduction of revenue, abolition of begar (forced labour) and social boycott of oppressive landlords, going beyond the official Congress programme. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, a militant guerrilla movement led by Alluri Sitaram Raju invoked Gandhi's name and the idea of Swaraj but resorted to methods far more radical than official non-violence, resisting the colonial forest laws that denied forest dwellers traditional grazing and gathering rights. Plantation workers in Assam, restricted from leaving tea gardens under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, saw freedom as the right to move freely and left the plantations to return to their home villages.

sections.title: 8. Chauri Chaura and the Withdrawal of Non-Cooperation (1922)
sections.content: By 1922, the movement had spread widely, but incidents of violence occurred in different places. In February 1922, in Chauri Chaura in Uttar Pradesh, a peaceful demonstration turned into a violent clash after local police fired on it, and in retaliation the enraged crowd set fire to the police station, killing all its occupants. On learning of this violence, Gandhi decided to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement, believing the satyagrahis had not been sufficiently trained for mass struggles that required strict adherence to non-violent discipline. This withdrawal disappointed many activists and marked the end of the first phase of mass nationalist mobilisation.

sections.title: 9. The Simon Commission and Purna Swaraj (1927-1929)
sections.content: In 1927, the British government set up the Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India and recommend changes, but as the Commission had no Indian members, it was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon' when it arrived in India in 1928. In an effort to win over moderate opinion, the viceroy Lord Irwin announced in October 1929 a vague offer of 'dominion status' for India in an unspecified future, which failed to satisfy the Congress. At its Lahore session in December 1929, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, the Indian National Congress formalised the demand for 'Purna Swaraj' or complete independence, and 26 January 1930 was declared as Independence Day, when people were to take a pledge to struggle for complete independence.

sections.title: 10. The Salt March and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)
sections.content: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation, since it was consumed by rich and poor alike and its production was a state monopoly under British law, making its manufacture by anyone other than the government a criminal offence. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi, along with 78 followers, set out from his ashram at Sabarmati on foot towards the Gujarati coastal town of Dandi, a distance of about 240 miles, reaching Dandi on 6 April and ceremonially violating the law by manufacturing salt by boiling sea water. This marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement, in which, unlike Non-Cooperation, people were now asked to not only refuse cooperation but also to actively break colonial laws.

sections.title: 11. Different Social Groups in the Civil Disobedience Movement
sections.content: Rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh participated actively in the movement, organising their communities since they had been hit hard by the trade depression and falling prices while revenue demands remained unchanged, though poorer peasants found it harder to pay rent and wanted it reduced too, sometimes joining more radical activities led by socialists and communists. Business classes, keen on protection against imported goods and a rupee-sterling exchange rate favourable to Indian trade, supported the Civil Disobedience Movement and gave financial assistance, though they were more wary of prolonged mass struggle. Industrial working classes did not participate in large numbers except in the Nagpur region, since Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands as it might alienate industrialists, and thousands of women also came out of their homes to listen to Gandhi, participate in protest marches, manufacture salt and picket foreign cloth and liquor shops.

sections.title: 12. The Sense of Collective Belonging: Icons, Images and History
sections.content: Nationalism also spread through the identification of icons and symbols, folklore, songs and popular practices that helped create a sense of collective belonging. The image of Bharat Mata, first painted by Abanindranath Tagore in the early twentieth century, portrayed India as a mother goddess figure, inspiring a feeling of a shared 'homeland' to fight for. Reinterpretation of history to emphasise the glorious achievements of ancient India, revival of Indian folklore, and the design of a tricolour flag (Swadeshi flag with eight lotuses representing eight provinces and a crescent moon representing Hindus and Muslims) during the Swadeshi movement, all helped nationalists build a shared sense of Indian identity distinct from colonial rule.

questions.model_answer: After presenting Viceroy Irwin with Eleven Demands that were rejected, Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930. It began dramatically with the Salt March, in which Gandhi and his followers walked about 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi to break the colonial salt law by making salt themselves. Unlike the Non-Cooperation Movement, this time people were asked to actively break specific unjust laws, not merely refuse cooperation - manufacturing salt, boycotting foreign cloth, and refusing to pay taxes. The movement saw wide participation from rich peasants, business groups seeking tariff protection, women who joined protests and picketing in large numbers, and in some regions tribal and poor peasants. Its significance lay in mobilising millions through a simple, symbolic act of defiance, drawing international attention to the freedom struggle, and eventually forcing the British government to negotiate through the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931.

questions.model_answer: The Kheda Satyagraha of 1917-18 supported peasants in Gujarat who were hit by crop failure and a plague epidemic, demanding relief from revenue payments. The Ahmedabad Satyagraha of 1918 supported cotton mill workers demanding better wages and working conditions. Together, these early successes established Gandhi's leadership and Satyagraha as an effective method of political mobilisation in India.

questions.question: What was the Simon Commission, and why was it opposed in India?

rubric.point: A statutory commission set up in 1927 to review India's constitutional system and recommend changes
Opposed because it had no Indian members, and was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon'

questions.model_answer: The Simon Commission was a statutory commission set up by the British government in 1927 to review India's constitutional system and recommend changes. It was opposed across India because it had no Indian members, and was greeted with black-flag demonstrations and the slogan 'Go back Simon' when it arrived in 1928.

questions.question: What did 'Purna Swaraj' mean, and when was it declared as the Congress's goal?

rubric.point: Meant complete independence, rejecting the vague offer of dominion status
Declared at the Lahore session in December 1929, with 26 January 1930 as the pledge day

questions.model_answer: 'Purna Swaraj' meant complete independence for India, rejecting the vague offer of 'dominion status' made by the Viceroy. It was formally declared as the Congress's goal at the Lahore session in December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, and 26 January 1930 was declared as the day for people to pledge to struggle for complete independence.

questions.question: Give two reasons why salt was chosen by Gandhi as a symbol for the Civil Disobedience Movement.

rubric.point: Salt was consumed by rich and poor alike, uniting people across all classes
Its production was a state monopoly, so manufacturing it was a criminal offence - breaking this law was symbolically powerful

questions.model_answer: Gandhi chose salt as a symbol because it was consumed by rich and poor alike, making it a cause that could unite all sections of Indian society. Its production was also a state monopoly under British law, so manufacturing salt without authorisation was a criminal offence, making the act of breaking this law a powerful and simple symbol of defiance against colonial rule.

questions.question: Explain the sequence of events from the Rowlatt Act to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

rubric.point: The Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed detention of political prisoners without trial
Gandhi called a nationwide hartal in protest; local leaders were arrested in Amritsar
On 13 April 1919, General Dyer opened fire on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds

questions.model_answer: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 gave the colonial government sweeping powers to detain political prisoners without trial. Gandhi launched a nationwide Satyagraha and hartal against the Act; alarmed by the response, local leaders were arrested in Amritsar. On 13 April 1919, a large crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, and General Dyer blocked the exits and ordered troops to open fire on the unarmed crowd, killing hundreds and shocking the nation.

questions.question: Why did Gandhi decide to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident?

rubric.point: In February 1922, a violent crowd set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura, killing its occupants
Gandhi believed satyagrahis were not sufficiently trained/disciplined for non-violent mass struggle
He called off the movement to prevent further violence, disappointing many activists

questions.model_answer: In February 1922, a peaceful demonstration at Chauri Chaura in Uttar Pradesh turned violent when the enraged crowd set fire to a police station, killing all its occupants. On learning of this violence, Gandhi decided to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement, believing that satyagrahis had not been sufficiently trained and disciplined for the kind of mass struggle that required strict non-violence, a decision that disappointed many activists.

questions.question: Describe how plantation workers in Assam interpreted the idea of freedom differently from the official Congress programme during the nationalist movement.

rubric.point: They were restricted from leaving tea gardens without permission under the Inland Emigration Act, 1859
For them, freedom meant the right to move freely, so they left the plantations to return to their villages
This went beyond the official Congress non-cooperation programme, showing a local, distinct interpretation of Swaraj

questions.model_answer: Plantation workers in Assam were restricted by the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 from leaving the tea gardens without permission. For them, freedom was closely bound up with the right to move freely, so when they heard of the Non-Cooperation Movement, many simply left the plantations and headed home to their villages. This action went well beyond the official Congress programme, showing that different social groups gave their own local meaning to the idea of Swaraj.

questions.question: Explain the significance of the Khilafat Movement for Hindu-Muslim unity in the national struggle.

rubric.point: Indian Muslims feared harsh treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War
A Khilafat Committee was formed under the leadership of the Ali brothers to defend the Khalifa's authority
Gandhi merged the Khilafat cause with Non-Cooperation to unite Hindus and Muslims in a common struggle

questions.model_answer: Indian Muslims were angered by rumours that a harsh peace treaty would be imposed on the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War, and formed a Khilafat Committee under the leadership of the Ali brothers to defend his authority. Gandhi saw this as an opportunity to bring Hindus and Muslims together under a common struggle, and merged the Khilafat cause with the Non-Cooperation Movement, strengthening Hindu-Muslim unity in the national movement.

questions.question: How was the image of the Indian nation constructed through cultural symbols like Bharat Mata and the tricolour flag?

rubric.point: Bharat Mata, painted by Abanindranath Tagore, portrayed India as a mother goddess, evoking emotional attachment to the homeland
A tricolour flag was designed during the Swadeshi movement, with symbols representing provinces and communities
These icons and symbols helped build a shared sense of collective national identity

questions.model_answer: The image of Bharat Mata, first painted by Abanindranath Tagore, portrayed India as a mother goddess figure, helping to build an emotional bond between Indians and their idea of the homeland. During the Swadeshi movement, a tricolour flag was designed, with symbols such as lotuses and a crescent moon representing different provinces and communities. Such icons and symbols played an important role in creating a shared sense of collective belonging to the Indian nation, distinct from colonial rule.

questions.topic: Gandhi's early Satyagrahas leading to Non-Cooperation
questions.question: Trace Gandhi's early experiments with Satyagraha in India (Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad) and explain how they prepared the ground for the Non-Cooperation Movement.

rubric.point: Satyagraha is based on the power of truth and non-violent resistance to injustice
Champaran, 1917: Gandhi supported indigo peasants against the oppressive plantation system
Kheda, 1917-18: supported peasants hit by crop failure/plague, demanding revenue relief
Ahmedabad, 1918: supported cotton mill workers demanding better wages
These successes established Gandhi's leadership and Satyagraha as a viable method, leading to the nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920

questions.model_answer: Gandhi's technique of Satyagraha was based on the power of truth and non-violent resistance to injustice. He first tested it in India in 1917 at Champaran, Bihar, where he supported peasants oppressed by the indigo plantation system. Later in 1917-18, he organised a Satyagraha in Kheda, Gujarat, to support peasants hit by crop failure and a plague epidemic, demanding revenue relief. In 1918, he organised a Satyagraha among cotton mill workers in Ahmedabad demanding better wages and working conditions. These early successes established Gandhi's leadership and Satyagraha as an effective and viable method of political mobilisation, paving the way for the launch of the nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920.

questions.topic: Diverse social groups in the national movement
questions.question: Explain how different social groups (peasants, tribals, business classes, women) participated in and interpreted the national movement in their own ways.

rubric.point: Peasants in Awadh, led by Baba Ramchandra, organised against talukdars and landlords, demanding lower rents/revenue
Tribal peasants in the Gudem Hills, led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, used militant methods invoking Gandhi's name and Swaraj
Business classes wanted protection against foreign imports and a favourable exchange rate, and gave financial support to the movement
Women participated in large numbers, joining protest marches, manufacturing salt and picketing foreign cloth/liquor shops
Each group interpreted Swaraj according to its own specific grievances, showing the movement was not uniform

questions.model_answer: Different social groups participated in the national movement with their own specific aspirations. In Awadh, peasants led by Baba Ramchandra organised against talukdars and landlords, demanding reduction of revenue and rent. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, tribal peasants led by Alluri Sitarama Raju invoked Gandhi's name and the idea of Swaraj but used far more militant, guerrilla methods against restrictive forest laws. Indian business classes, seeking protection against foreign imports and a favourable exchange rate for trade, extended financial support to the movement. Women also came out in large numbers, joining protest marches, manufacturing salt, and picketing shops selling foreign cloth and liquor. Together, these examples show that different social groups interpreted and pursued the idea of Swaraj according to their own local grievances, rather than following a single, uniform programme.

questions.topic: Social groups in Civil Disobedience Movement
questions.question: Describe any four ways in which different social groups participated in the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34).

rubric.point: Rich peasants (e.g. Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP) joined actively since they were hit hard by trade depression and high revenue demand, and organised their communities
Poor peasants wanted freedom from payment of rent, and some joined radical movements led by socialists and communists, going beyond the Congress programme
Indian business classes wanted protection against imports and a rupee-sterling exchange rate favourable to Indian trade, and gave financial support to the movement

Women participated in large numbers, joining protest marches, manufacturing salt and picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops, though the Congress was initially reluctant to allow women in the movement

questions.model_answer: Different social groups joined the Civil Disobedience Movement with their own aspirations. Rich peasants, such as the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh, participated actively because they were hit hard by falling prices and fixed high revenue demands during the trade depression, and they mobilised their communities into the movement. Poor peasants wanted freedom from payment of rent to landlords, and in some areas joined more radical activities led by socialists and communists, going beyond the Congress's official non-violent programme. Indian business classes, keen on protection against foreign imports and a more favourable exchange rate for Indian trade, extended financial support to the movement. Women also participated in large numbers, joining protest marches, helping manufacture salt, and picketing shops selling foreign cloth and liquor, even though the Congress was initially reluctant to allow women into active protest.

questions.topic: Constructing the idea of the nation
questions.question: Explain any four ways in which the sense of collective belonging to the Indian nation was created through culture and symbols.

rubric.point: The identification of India with the image of Bharat Mata, a mother goddess figure, helped build a shared emotional bond with the nation
Revival and reinterpretation of Indian folklore, myths and songs (e.g. by Natesa Sastri) helped project a true, pure national culture uncorrupted by outside influences
Icons and symbols, such as the tricolour flag designed during the Swadeshi movement, played a role in unifying people under a shared identity
Reinterpretation of history to celebrate India's great achievements and glorious past gave Indians pride and a sense of shared identity against colonial rule

questions.model_answer: A sense of collective belonging to India as a nation came partly through the identification of the country with the image of Bharat Mata, a mother goddess figure that evoked a shared emotional bond among Indians. Nationalists also revived and reinterpreted Indian folklore, collecting folk tales and songs, as done by figures like Natesa Sastri, to project the idea of a true, pure national culture untouched by outside influence. Icons and symbols also played a unifying role - for instance, a tricolour flag was designed during the Swadeshi movement, becoming a symbol of resistance and shared identity. Finally, nationalist writers reinterpreted history to highlight India's glorious achievements in the past, instilling pride and a sense of belonging to counter the humiliation of colonial rule.

subquestions.question: Explain how print culture (pamphlets, newspapers, printed images) helped spread nationalist ideas among people from different regions and backgrounds during India's freedom struggle.

This helped create a shared, collective identity - an 'imagined community' - by giving diverse people common symbols, stories and songs to identify with, even without direct personal contact

subquestions.model_answer: Print culture allowed nationalist images (like Bharat Mata), songs, poems and stories to be reproduced cheaply and circulated widely, reaching people across very different regions and backgrounds who would otherwise never interact directly. questions.question: Provide evidence to support the claim that print culture helped in the growth of nationalism in India.

questions.model_answer: Despite repressive colonial measures aimed at controlling the press, nationalist newspapers grew steadily in number across all parts of India; they reported on colonial misrule and actively encouraged nationalist activity. Colonial attempts to throttle this nationalist press criticism provoked militant protest, which in turn led to renewed cycles of persecution and protest. A clear example is Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who wrote sympathetically in his newspaper Kesari about Punjab revolutionaries deported in 1907 - this led to his own imprisonment in 1908, which provoked widespread protests all across India, showing how print culture actively fuelled and sustained the nationalist movement.

questions.topic: Significance and milestones of the Civil Disobedience Movement
questions.question: Examine the significance and key milestones of the Civil Disobedience Movement that took place in India during the struggle for independence.

rubric.point: Key milestones: the Dandi March (Gandhi's 240-mile march to produce salt) became a powerful symbol of resistance with international attention; British repression and mass arrests followed, which fuelled public outrage and strengthened the movement; the movement eventually led to negotiations between Congress and the British government, though it fell short of full independence

Significance: mass participation across diverse sections of society showed unity and determination; Indians boycotted British goods to promote self-reliance and protest colonial economic policy; the movement raised awareness and inspired active nationalist participation across the masses; its legacy as a symbol of non-violent resistance went on to inspire freedom movements worldwide

questions.model_answer: Key milestones of the Civil Disobedience Movement include the Dandi March, in which Gandhi's 240-mile march to produce salt became a powerful symbol of resistance and drew international attention; the British response of repression and mass arrests, which fuelled public outrage and further strengthened the movement; and the eventual negotiations between the Congress and the British government that the movement led to, though these fell short of achieving full independence. The movement's significance lies in its mass participation - it saw widespread involvement from diverse segments of Indian society, showcasing unity and determination; the boycott of British goods, through which Indians promoted self-reliance and protested colonial economic policy; the way it raised nationalist awareness and inspired active participation and unity among the masses; and its lasting legacy as a symbol of non-violent resistance, which went on to inspire freedom movements worldwide.

questions.topic: Satyagraha and the constitutional Right to Protest
questions.question: The Constitution of India guarantees the fundamental right to protest, derived from the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to assemble peacefully - though this is subject to reasonable restrictions, and violent actions during protest are seen as violating citizens' fundamental duties, so the right to protest is understood to cover only peaceful demonstrations. Examine the elements of Satyagraha employed during the 20th-century Indian freedom struggle in light of their alignment with this constitutional Right to Protest.

rubric.point: Elements of Satyagraha that align with the modern right to protest include its emphasis on non-violence, peaceful protest, respect for human rights, and dialogue/negotiation with authorities - these promote democratic values, freedom of speech, and the right to dissent, matching the constitutional protection for peaceful protest

However, certain elements of Satyagraha may sit in tension with the constitution: acts of civil disobedience that involved deliberately breaking specific laws (like the salt law) or disrupting public order could be seen as conflicting with the principle of upholding the rule of law, and techniques that obstructed essential services or government functioning could be considered constitutionally problematic today

questions.model_answer: Many elements of Satyagraha as practised in the freedom struggle align closely with the constitutional Right to Protest: its core emphasis on non-violence, peaceful demonstration, respect for human dignity, and preference for dialogue and negotiation over confrontation all promote the same democratic values - freedom of speech and expression and the right to dissent - that the Constitution protects. At the same time, some elements of Satyagraha sit in tension with a strict reading of today's constitutional right: deliberate acts of civil disobedience, such as breaking specific laws (like the colonial salt law) or disrupting public order, can be seen as conflicting with the principle of upholding the rule of law; similarly, techniques that obstructed essential services or hindered the functioning of government machinery could be viewed as going beyond what the constitutionally protected right to peaceful protest allows. So while Satyagraha's spirit of peaceful, principled dissent strongly echoes the modern Right to Protest, its more disruptive tactics of lawbreaking would need to be reconciled with the constitution's insistence on peaceful, lawful demonstration.

questions.topic: Case study - Gandhiji's 'Do or Die' speech (Quit India Movement)

I am not going to be satisfied with anything short of complete freedom... Here is a mantra, a short one, that I give you... The mantra is: Do or Die. We shall either free India or die in the attempt; we shall not live to see the perpetuation of our slavery... Let that be your pledge.'

subquestions.question: Discuss the economic context and political climate that led to the adoption of the 'Do or Die' mantra.

rubric.point: Economic context: the harsh impact of the Second World War on the Indian economy and living conditions (price rises, shortages) created widespread discontent among Indians

Political context: the British government's failure to fulfil promises of dominion status after the war left Indian leaders disillusioned with incremental reforms, and the political climate grew tense with growing impatience for complete independence, leading Gandhi to seek a more decisive strategy to break the negotiating stalemate

subquestions.model_answer: Economically, the Second World War had a harsh impact on India's economy and living conditions, causing widespread discontent among ordinary Indians. Politically, the British government's failure to fulfil earlier promises of dominion status for India after the war left Indian leaders deeply disillusioned with the strategy of pursuing incremental reforms through negotiation. With the political climate growing increasingly tense and public impatience for full independence mounting, Gandhi sought a more decisive strategy to break the stalemate in negotiations with the British - leading to the adoption of the uncompromising 'Do or Die' mantra.

Thousands came to hear Gandhi wherever he stopped, and he explained what he meant by swaraj and urged them to peacefully defy the British. On 6 April, he reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law by manufacturing salt from sea water.

questions.topic: Case study - Print and Censorship in colonial India (First and Second World Wars)
questions.passage:
Print and Censorship
The power of the printed word is most often seen in the way governments seek to regulate and suppress print. The colonial government kept continuous track of all books and newspapers published in India and passed numerous laws to control the press.
During the First World War, under the Defence of India Rules, 22 newspapers had to furnish securities. Of these, 18 shut down rather than comply with government orders. The Sedition Committee Report under Rowlatt in 1919 further strengthened controls that led to imposition of penalties on various newspapers. At the outbreak of the Second World War, the 'Defence of India Act' was passed, allowing censoring of reports of war-related topics. All reports about the Quit India Movement came under its purview. In August 1942, about 90 newspapers were suppressed.

rubric.point: they were reporting on the Quit India Movement, which came under the purview of the Defence of India Act allowing censorship of war-related reports

subquestions.model_answer: Because they carried reports on the Quit India Movement, which came under the purview of the Defence of India Act that allowed the government to censor reports on war-related and movement-related topics.

subquestions.question: How did the colonial government's policies affect nationalism?

rubric.point: press-control laws tried to suppress nationalist news/ideas from reaching the public, but many papers defied government orders and shut down rather than comply, showing continued nationalist resistance

subquestions.model_answer: The government's repeated press-control laws tried to restrict nationalist ideas and news of movements from reaching the public and to weaken support for the freedom struggle. However, many newspapers defied these orders and chose to shut down rather than comply, showing that nationalist resistance continued despite censorship.

subquestions.question: Examine the role of the press in colonial India.

rubric.point: the press published nationalist ideas and spread news of movements, mobilising public opinion against colonial rule

because of this, the government repeatedly tried to track, license and censor the press through laws like the Defence of India Rules, the Sedition Committee/Rowlatt Report and the Defence of India Act, showing it saw the press as a serious threat

subquestions.model_answer: The press in colonial India published nationalist ideas and spread news of movements like the Quit India Movement, helping mobilise public opinion against colonial rule. questions.topic: Case study - First World War and Indian industry
questions.passage:
Yet, till the First World War, industrial growth was slow. The war created a dramatically new situation. With British mills busy with war production to meet the needs of the army, Manchester imports into India declined. Suddenly, Indian mills had a vast home market to supply. As the war prolonged, Indian factories were called upon to supply war needs: jute bags, cloth for army uniforms, tents and leather boots, horse and mule saddles and a host of other items. New factories were set up and old ones ran multiple shifts. Many new workers were employed and everyone was made to work longer hours. Over the war years industrial production boomed.
After the war, Manchester could never recapture its old position in the Indian market. Unable to modernise and compete with the US, Germany and Japan, the economy of Britain crumbled after the war. Cotton production collapsed and exports of cotton cloth from Britain fell dramatically. Within the colonies, local industrialists gradually consolidated their position, substituting foreign manufacturers and capturing the home market.

Meanwhile, Indian industrialists had used the war years to consolidate their position and capture the home market, substituting for foreign manufacturers, so Manchester could not regain its old share.

new factories were set up and old ones expanded to multiple shifts, creating employment for many new workers and strengthening Indian industry's position even after the war

questions.topic: Case study - Print and Censorship under the East India Company (1798-1835)
questions.passage:
Before 1798, the colonial state under the East India Company was not too concerned with censorship. Strangely, its early measures to control printed matter were directed against Englishmen in India who were critical of Company misrule and hated the actions of particular Company officers. The Company was worried that such criticisms might be used by its critics in England to attack its trade monopoly in India.
By the 1820s, the Calcutta Supreme Court passed certain regulations to control press freedom and the Company began encouraging publication of newspapers that would celebrate British rule. In 1835, faced with urgent petitions by editors of English and vernacular newspapers, Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise press laws. Thomas Macaulay, a liberal colonial official, formulated new rules that restored the earlier freedoms.
